claim: Cholesterol is a major structural component of the plasma membrane (PM).
source: Cholesterol is a major structural component of the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cholesterol's role in cellular membranes.

claim: The majority of PM cholesterol forms complexes with other PM lipids, making it inaccessible for intracellular transport.
source: The majority of PM cholesterol forms complexes with other PM lipids, making it inaccessible for intracellular transport.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge about cholesterol sequestration in membranes.

claim: GRAMD1s are endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-anchored lipid transfer proteins.
source: We show that endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-anchored lipid transfer proteins, the GRAMD1s, sense and transport accessible PM cholesterol to the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: GRAMD1s sense and transport accessible PM cholesterol to the ER.
source: We show that endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-anchored lipid transfer proteins, the GRAMD1s, sense and transport accessible PM cholesterol to the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches including live-cell imaging, biochemical assays, and knockout cell analysis.

claim: GRAMD1s bind to one another and populate ER-PM contacts by sensing a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol via their GRAM domains.
source: GRAMD1s bind to one another and populate ER-PM contacts by sensing a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol via their GRAM domains.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1D-E) and live-cell imaging showing recruitment to ER-PM contacts (Figure 3).

claim: GRAMD1s facilitate the transport of accessible cholesterol via their StART-like domains.
source: They then facilitate the transport of this cholesterol via their StART-like domains.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid transfer assays (Figure 5) and rescue experiments with StART-like domain mutants.

claim: Cells that lack all three GRAMD1s exhibit striking expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol.
source: Cells that lack all three GRAMD1s exhibit striking expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol as a result of less efficient PM to ER transport of accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by D4H binding assays in GRAMD1 TKO cells (Figure 7A-B).

claim: The expansion of accessible PM cholesterol in GRAMD1 TKO cells results from less efficient PM to ER transport of accessible cholesterol.
source: Cells that lack all three GRAMD1s exhibit striking expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol as a result of less efficient PM to ER transport of accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This is supported by SREBP-2 cleavage assays (Figure 6B-C) and D4 binding time-course experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: Sterol represents ~20% of total cellular lipids in metazoans.
source: In metazoans, cholesterol represents ~20% of total cellular lipids and is therefore essential for the structural integrity of cellular membranes and for cell physiology (van Meer et al., 2008; Vance, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Between 60% and 80% of total cellular cholesterol is concentrated in the plasma membrane.
source: Between 60% and 80% of total cellular cholesterol is concentrated in the plasma membrane (PM), where it represents up to ~45% of total lipids in this bilayer (de Duve, 1971; Lange et al., 1989; Ray et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol in the PM represents up to ~45% of total lipids in this bilayer.
source: Between 60% and 80% of total cellular cholesterol is concentrated in the plasma membrane (PM), where it represents up to ~45% of total lipids in this bilayer (de Duve, 1971; Lange et al., 1989; Ray et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cellular cholesterol levels are maintained by regulated delivery and production, primarily through receptor-mediated endocytosis of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs).
source: Cellular cholesterol levels are maintained by regulated delivery and production, primarily through receptor-mediated endocytosis of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) (Goldstein and Brown, 2015) and de novo synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that is controlled by the activation of SREBP transcription factors (Brown et al., 2018; Goldstein and Brown, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: De novo cholesterol synthesis in the ER is controlled by the activation of SREBP transcription factors.
source: Cellular cholesterol levels are maintained by regulated delivery and production, primarily through receptor-mediated endocytosis of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) (Goldstein and Brown, 2015) and de novo synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that is controlled by the activation of SREBP transcription factors (Brown et al., 2018; Goldstein and Brown, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most cholesterol in the PM is sequestered, but a small fraction of PM cholesterol (~15% of PM lipids) remains accessible for extraction and transport.
source: Most cholesterol in the PM is sequestered, but a small fraction of PM cholesterol (~15% of PM lipids) remains accessible for extraction and transport (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: GRAMD1s possess an N-terminal GRAM domain and a C-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: GRAMDs (namely GRAMD1a, GRAMD1b, GRAMD1c, GRAMD2, and GRAMD3) all possess an N-terminal GRAM domain and a C-terminal transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is shown in the domain structure diagram (Figure 1A).

claim: The three GRAMD1 proteins (GRAMD1s) possess a StART-like domain.
source: In addition, the three GRAMD1 proteins (GRAMD1s) possess a StART-like domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the domain structure diagram (Figure 1A).

claim: GRAMD1s are enriched in discrete patches along ER tubules.
source: Analysis of COS-7 cells expressing individual EGFP-tagged GRAMD1s or GRAMD3 (EGFP-GRAMD1a, EGFP-GRAMD1b, EGFP-GRAMD1c, or EGFP-GRAMD3) and a general ER marker (RFP-tagged Sec61β) revealed enrichment of GRAMD1s and GRAMD3 in similar discrete patches along ER tubules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images (Figure 1B).

claim: GRAMD1s form homo- and heteromeric complexes.
source: These results demonstrate that these proteins form both homo- and heteromeric complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1D-E).

claim: The luminal helix of GRAMD1b is predicted to be an amphipathic helix.
source: Furthermore, helical wheel analysis of the luminal helix from GRAMD1b predicted that this protein contained an amphipathic helix, with charged and hydrophobic amino acids occupying opposite sides of the helix (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using helical wheel analysis.

claim: The luminal helix is necessary for GRAMD1b to form discrete patches on tubular ER.
source: Whereas GRAMD1b (wild-type control) formed patches on tubular ER, both GRAMD1b (Δhelix) and GRAMD1b (5E) exhibited diffuse localization patterns, with fewer discrete patches on tubular ER (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy of mutant constructs (Figure 2C).

claim: The interaction between luminal helices depends on the hydrophobic surface of GRAMD1b.
source: Blue native PAGE analysis (BN-PAGE) of the purified proteins revealed that wild-type helices migrated slower than the 5E mutants, indicating that interaction between luminal helices depended on the hydrophobic surface of GRAMD1b (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BN-PAGE analysis (Figure 2E).

claim: Both transmembrane domains and luminal helices contribute to the formation of GRAMD1 complexes.
source: Thus, both transmembrane domains and luminal helices contributed to the formation of GRAMD1 complexes (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with various mutants (Figure 2F-G).

claim: Cholesterol loading leads to the accumulation of GRAMD1s at ER–PM contact sites.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that 'cholesterol loading' leads to the accumulation of GRAMD1s at ER–PM contact sites (Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own experiments (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Within 20 min of treating cells with a complex of cholesterol and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (cholesterol/MCD), GRAMD1b was recruited to the PM.
source: Within 20 min of treating cells with a complex of cholesterol and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (cholesterol/MCD), GRAMD1b was indeed recruited to the PM (Figure 3A,B; Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy time-course experiments (Figure 3A-B).

claim: GRAMD1a, GRAMD1c, and GRAMD3 were all recruited to ER–PM contacts upon cholesterol loading.
source: In addition, we found that GRAMD1a, GRAMD1c, and GRAMD3 were all recruited to ER–PM contacts upon cholesterol loading, with kinetics similar to GRAMD1b recruitment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy time-course experiments (Figure 3B).

claim: A version of GRAMD1b that lacked the GRAM domain (GRAMD1b ΔGRAM) failed to localize to the PM upon cholesterol loading.
source: However, a version of GRAMD1b that lacked the GRAM domain (GRAMD1b ΔGRAM) failed to localize to the PM, even after 30 min, indicating the essential role of this domain in sensing PM cholesterol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments with the ΔGRAM mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The GRAM domain of GRAMD1b did not bind liposomes when the liposome contained only phosphatidylcholine.
source: The GRAM domain did not bind liposomes when the liposome contained only phosphatidylcholine (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays (Figure 3C).

claim: The GRAM domain bound liposomes that contained free cholesterol, although such binding was rather weak.
source: By contrast, the GRAM domain bound liposomes that contained free cholesterol, although such binding was rather weak, and only ~25% of purified GRAM domains bound liposomes even when the liposome contained high levels of cholesterol (Chol) (60%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Strong binding of the GRAM domain to liposomes was observed when 50% cholesterol and 20% phosphatidylserine were both present in the liposomes.
source: However, strong binding was observed when 50% cholesterol and 20% phosphatidylserine were both present in the liposomes (~80% of the GRAM domains bound to liposomes) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays (Figure 3C).

claim: The addition of free cholesterol dramatically enhanced binding of the GRAM domain to phosphatidylserine-containing membranes.
source: Thus, the addition of free cholesterol dramatically enhanced binding of the GRAM domain to phosphatidylserine-containing membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays comparing different lipid compositions (Figure 3C).

claim: The GRAM domain acts as a coincidence detector of unsequestered/accessible cholesterol and anionic lipids in the PM.
source: These results indicate that the recruitment of GRAMD1s to the PM is regulated by interactions between GRAM domains and anionic lipids, and that these interactions are enhanced by the additional presence of accessible/unsequestered cholesterol in the PM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays with various lipid combinations (Figure 3C-F).

claim: When liposomes contained 25% sphingomyelin, the percentage of GRAMD1b GRAM domains that bound to the liposomes decreased from ~80% to ~45%.
source: When these liposomes contained 25% sphingomyelin, the percentage of GRAMD1b GRAM domains that bound to the liposomes decreased from ~80% to ~45% (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays with sphingomyelin (Figure 3E).

claim: Within 30 min of sphingomyelinase treatment, GRAMD1b was recruited to the PM.
source: Within 30 min of sphingomyelinase treatment, GRAMD1b was indeed recruited to the PM (Figure 3G), albeit this recruitment was less efficient than cholesterol loading to the PM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments (Figure 3G).

claim: EGFP-tagged GRAMD1 GRAM domains (EGFP–GRAM1a, EGFP–GRAM1b, and EGFP–GRAM1c) were all recruited to the PM upon sphingomyelinase treatment.
source: EGFP-tagged GRAMD1 GRAM domains (namely EGFP–GRAM1a, EGFP–GRAM1b, and EGFP–GRAM1c) were all recruited to the PM upon sphingomyelinase treatment (Figure 3H), revealing a direct role of the GRAM domain in detecting the unsequestered/accessible pool of PM cholesterol in cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments (Figure 3H).

claim: Two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b double knockout cell clones (DKO #38 and DKO #40) were selected.
source: After transfection of plasmids expressing GRAMD1-specific guide RNAs and Cas9 protein, two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b double knockout cell clones (DKO #38 and DKO #40) and two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b/1c triple knockout cell clones (TKO #1 and TKO #15) were selected.
evidence: This describes the experimental generation of knockout cell lines.

claim: Two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b/1c triple knockout cell clones (TKO #1 and TKO #15) were selected.
source: After transfection of plasmids expressing GRAMD1-specific guide RNAs and Cas9 protein, two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b double knockout cell clones (DKO #38 and DKO #40) and two independent isolates of GRAMD1a/1b/1c triple knockout cell clones (TKO #1 and TKO #15) were selected.
evidence: This describes the experimental generation of knockout cell lines.

claim: The absence of GRAMD1a and GRAMD1b was confirmed by western blotting and genomic sequencing.
source: The absence of GRAMD1a and GRAMD1b was confirmed by western blotting and genomic sequencing (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting and sequencing data (Figure 4B).

claim: No obvious defects in cell viability or overall morphology were observed for GRAMD1 knockout cells, with the exception that KO cells grew slightly slower than parental HeLa cells.
source: No obvious defects in cell viability or overall morphology were observed for these KO cells, with the exception that KO cells grew slightly slower than parental HeLa cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the characterization of knockout cell lines.

claim: Treatment with sphingomyelinase for 1 hr led to only modest recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in wild-type HeLa cells.
source: Treatment with sphingomyelinase for 1 hr led to only modest recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in wild-type HeLa cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy (Figure 4D).

claim: The same sphingomyelinase treatment lead to much more prominent recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in GRAMD1 TKO cells.
source: By contrast, the same treatment lead to much more prominent recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in GRAMD1 TKO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy (Figure 4D).

claim: PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b upon sphingomyelinase treatment was significantly enhanced in GRAMD1 TKO cells, compared to wild-type control cells.
source: TIRF microscopy of cells expressing EGFP–GRAM1b revealed that PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b upon sphingomyelinase treatment was significantly enhanced in GRAMD1 TKO cells, compared to wild-type control cells, over the entire 1 hr treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy quantification (Figure 4E).

claim: Additional treatment of GRAMD1 TKO cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MCD) resulted in acute loss of the PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b within 2 min.
source: Importantly, additional treatment of GRAMD1 TKO cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MCD), which extracts cholesterol from cellular membranes, resulted in acute loss of the PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b within 2 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of whole-cell and purified PM lipid extracts from wild-type control and GRAMD1 TKO HeLa cells did not reveal significant changes in cholesterol and other major lipids, except for very minor increases in cholesterol esters.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of whole-cell and purified PM lipid extracts from wild-type control and GRAMD1 TKO HeLa cells did not reveal significant changes in cholesterol and other major lipids, except for very minor increases in cholesterol esters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomics analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-D).

claim: GRAMD1s are not essential for maintaining total levels of PM cholesterol.
source: Thus, GRAMD1s are not essential for maintaining total levels of PM cholesterol.
evidence: This is inferred from the lipidomics data showing no significant changes in total PM cholesterol in TKO cells.

claim: GRAMD1a StART-like domains transferred DHE most efficiently, at a rate corresponding to ~8 DHE molecules per minute.
source: GRAMD1a StART-like domains transferred DHE most efficiently, at a rate corresponding to ~8 DHE molecules per minute.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET-based lipid transfer assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: GRAMD1b and GRAMD1c transported ~1 DHE molecule per minute.
source: In comparison, GRAMD1b and GRAMD1c transported ~1 DHE molecule per minute, as calculated using a standard curve (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET-based lipid transfer assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Purified GRAMD1a and GRAMD1b StART-like domains with 5P mutations were unable to transfer DHE in vitro.
source: Purified GRAMD1a and GRAMD1b StART-like domains with 5P mutations were unable to transfer DHE in vitro (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET-based lipid transfer assays (Figure 5C-D).

claim: The enhanced PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b in GRAMD1 TKO cells was dramatically suppressed by expressing wild-type mRuby–GRAMD1b but not by expressing a mutant version of mRuby–GRAMD1b that is defective in cholesterol transport [mRuby–GRAMD1b (5P)].
source: Strikingly, the enhanced PM recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b was dramatically suppressed by expressing wild-type mRuby–GRAMD1b but not by expressing a mutant version of mRuby–GRAMD1b that is defective in cholesterol transport [mRuby–GRAMD1b (5P)] (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy rescue experiments (Figure 5E).

claim: PM recruitment of mRuby–GRAMD1b upon sphingomyelinase treatment of TKO cells was higher for the 5P mutant GRAMD1b than for wild-type GRAMD1b.
source: By contrast, PM recruitment of mRuby–GRAMD1b upon sphingomyelinase treatment of TKO cells was higher for the 5P mutant GRAMD1b than for wild-type GRAMD1b (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments (Figure 5F).

claim: Overexpression of STARD4, OSBP, ORP4, and ORP9 did not suppress the enhanced recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in TKO cells upon sphingomyelinase treatment.
source: However, their expression did not suppress the enhanced recruitment of EGFP–GRAM1b to the PM in TKO cells upon sphingomyelinase treatment, being unable to substitute the function of GRAMD1s (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,D; compare with Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments with other cholesterol transfer proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,D).

claim: TIRF microscopy of cells expressing EGFP–GRAMD1b revealed that sphingomyelinase treatment led to sustained recruitment of GRAMD1b to the PM (during 3 hr of imaging).
source: TIRF microscopy of cells expressing EGFP–GRAMD1b revealed that sphingomyelinase treatment led to sustained recruitment of GRAMD1b to the PM (during 3 hr of imaging) (Figure 6A; Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by long-term TIRF microscopy time-course (Figure 6A).

claim: Suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage was observed in control cell lysates within 90 min of sphingomyelinase treatment.
source: Suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage was observed in control cell lysates within 90 min; however, such suppression was delayed and reduced (but not eliminated) in TKO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting for SREBP-2 (Figure 6B-C).

claim: Suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage upon sphingomyelinase treatment was delayed and reduced (but not eliminated) in GRAMD1 TKO cells compared to control cells.
source: Suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage was observed in control cell lysates within 90 min; however, such suppression was delayed and reduced (but not eliminated) in TKO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting for SREBP-2 (Figure 6B-C).

claim: Re-expression of GRAMD1b in TKO cells was sufficient to suppress SREBP-2 cleavage to an extent similar to that observed in wild-type control cells at the 180 min time point.
source: Importantly, re-expression of GRAMD1b in TKO cells was sufficient to suppress SREBP-2 cleavage to an extent similar to that observed in wild-type control cells at the 180 min time point, thereby rescuing the phenotype (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting for SREBP-2 in rescue experiments (Figure 6D-E).

claim: The expression of GRAMD1b ΔGRAM or GRAMD1b 5P in TKO cells failed to rescue the reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage phenotype.
source: The expression of GRAMD1b ΔGRAM or GRAMD1b 5P in TKO cells failed to rescue the phenotype (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting for SREBP-2 in rescue experiments with mutants (Figure 6D).

claim: TKO cells showed continuous increase in binding of EGFP–D4 to the PM even after 180 min of sphingomyelinase treatment.
source: TKO cells, however, showed continuous increase in binding of EGFP–D4 to the PM even after 180 min (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B), suggesting a sustained accumulation of accessible cholesterol in the PM of TKO cells, due to less efficient transport of accessible cholesterol from the PM to the ER, that does not occur in wild-type control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by D4 binding assays over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B).

claim: GRAMD1b TM swap failed to rescue the reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage observed in GRAMD1 TKO cells.
source: Remarkably, GRAMD1b TM swap failed to rescue the reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage observed in GRAMD1 TKO cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting for SREBP-2 in rescue experiments (Figure 6E).

claim: GRAMD1b TM swap remained diffusely distributed on the tubular ER even at the end of the 180 min imaging period.
source: GRAMD1b TM swap remained diffusely distributed on the tubular ER (which is closely attached to the PM) even at the end of the 180 min imaging period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Wild-type GRAMD1b progressively accumulated at ER–PM contacts as discrete patches with much stronger PM recruitment compared to GRAMD1b TM swap.
source: By contrast, wild-type GRAMD1b progressively accumulated at ER–PM contacts as discrete patches with much stronger PM recruitment (Figure 6F,G; Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy (Figure 6F-G).

claim: EGFP–D4H proteins bound more strongly to the PM of GRAMD1 TKO cells compared to that of control cells.
source: Strikingly, EGFP–D4H proteins bound more strongly to the PM of GRAMD1 TKO cells compared to that of control cells (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Pre-treatment of GRAMD1 TKO cells with MCD for 30 min resulted in loss of the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM.
source: Pre-treatment of GRAMD1 TKO cells with MCD for 30 min resulted in loss of the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), validating the specificity of this probe in sensing the accessible pool of PM cholesterol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding after MCD treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: Re-expression of any of the three GRAMD1s in TKO cells was sufficient to reduce the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM.
source: Re-expression of any of the three GRAMD1s in TKO cells was sufficient to reduce the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM, thereby rescuing the chronic expansion of the D4H-accessible pool of PM cholesterol observed in TKO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding in rescue experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C).

claim: All mutant versions of GRAMD1b, including Y430A/V445A, 5P and T469D mutants, failed to reduce the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM of TKO cells.
source: All mutant versions of GRAMD1b, including a newly designed mutant in which the hydrophobicity of the surface of the sterol-binding pocket is changed (Y430A, V445A), as well as 5P and T469D mutants, failed to reduce the binding of EGFP–D4H to the PM of TKO cells because they are unable to rescue the chronic expansion of the D4H-accessible pool of PM cholesterol in TKO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding in rescue experiments with mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E-I).

claim: Rapamycin-induced PM recruitment of the chimeric GRAMD1b protein led to acute reduction in D4H-accessible PM cholesterol in GRAMD1 TKO cells within 60 min.
source: Strikingly, rapamycin-induced PM recruitment of the chimeric GRAMD1b protein led to acute reduction in D4H-accessible PM cholesterol in GRAMD1 TKO cells within 60 min, reducing the binding of EGFP–D4H proteins to the PM (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding after rapamycin-induced recruitment (Figure 7E-F).

claim: Recruitment of mutant versions of miRFP-FKBP–GRAMD1b (5P and T469D mutants) did not reduce the PM EGFP–D4H signal.
source: However, recruitment of the mutant versions did not reduce the PM EGFP–D4H signal (Figure 7F), demonstrating a critical role for StART-like domain-dependent PM to ER cholesterol transport in the removal of the expanded pool of accessible PM cholesterol by GRAMD1b at ER–PM contact sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy with D4H binding after rapamycin-induced recruitment of mutants (Figure 7F).

claim: GRAMD1s play a direct role in facilitating the transport of accessible PM cholesterol to the ER at ER–PM contact sites.
source: On the basis of these results, we conclude that GRAMD1s play a direct role in facilitating the transport of accessible PM cholesterol to the ER at ER–PM contact sites.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the rapamycin-induced recruitment experiments showing that forced recruitment of GRAMD1b to ER-PM contacts reduces accessible PM cholesterol.

claim: GRAMD1s contribute to PM cholesterol homeostasis by sensing a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol and facilitating its transport to the ER at ER–PM contact sites.
source: We have demonstrated that the evolutionarily conserved family of ER-anchored GRAMD1s contribute to PM cholesterol homeostasis by sensing a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol and facilitating its transport to the ER at ER–PM contact sites.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: GRAMD1s and GRAMD3 form homo- and heteromeric complexes and localize to discrete patches on tubular ER in mammalian cells at rest.
source: We found that GRAMD1s and GRAMD3 form homo- and heteromeric complexes and localize to discrete patches on tubular ER in mammalian cells at rest.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and microscopy experiments (Figures 1-2).

claim: The transmembrane domains and luminal helices of GRAMD1s mediate the formation of protein–protein complexes.
source: We identified that their transmembrane domains and luminal helices, which are predicted to form amphipathic surfaces, mediated the formation of protein–protein complexes and regulated their progressive recruitment to ER–PM contacts and their functions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2).

claim: The GRAM domain of GRAMD1s acts as a coincidence detector, tuned to the presence of both 'unsequestered/accessible' cholesterol and anionic lipids, including phosphatidylserine, in the PM.
source: Using in vitro liposome sedimentation assays and live-cell imaging, we found that the GRAM domain of GRAMD1s acts as a coincidence detector, tuned to the presence of both 'unsequestered/accessible' cholesterol and anionic lipids, including phosphatidylserine, in the PM (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays and live-cell imaging (Figure 3).

claim: The binding of the GRAM domain to membranes requires that unsequestered/accessible cholesterol exceeds a certain threshold.
source: Importantly, the binding of the GRAM domain to membranes requires that unsequestered/accessible cholesterol exceeds a certain threshold.
evidence: This is demonstrated by liposome sedimentation assays showing dose-dependent binding (Figure 3C-F).

claim: GRAMD1s sense a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol through their GRAM domain and facilitate its transport through their StART-like domain.
source: We found that GRAMD1s sense a transient expansion of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol through their GRAM domain and facilitate its transport through their StART-like domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experiments including GRAM domain recruitment assays and StART-like domain lipid transfer assays.

claim: Disruption of GRAMD1 functions leads to less efficient transport of accessible cholesterol from the PM to the ER and reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage.
source: Disruption of their functions leads to less efficient transport of accessible PM cholesterol to the ER and reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SREBP-2 cleavage assays in TKO cells (Figure 6B-C).

claim: The formation of GRAMD1 protein complexes is critical for the cellular functions of GRAMD1s in vivo.
source: Using structure–function analysis, we demonstrated that GRAMD1s couple their PM-sensing property and cholesterol-transport function via their GRAM and StART-like domains, and that GRAMD1 complex formation ensures the progressive recruitment of GRAMD1 proteins to ER–PM contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the TM swap mutant that cannot form complexes (Figure 6E-G).

claim: Removal of accessible PM cholesterol occurs within ~1 hr when re-expressed GRAMD1 proteins are artificially recruited to ER–PM contact sites in GRAMD1 TKO cells.
source: Our results demonstrate that removal of accessible PM cholesterol occurs within ~1 hr, when re-expressed GRAMD1 proteins are artificially recruited to ER–PM contact sites to facilitate transport of accessible cholesterol from the PM to the ER in GRAMD1 TKO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rapamycin-induced recruitment experiments (Figure 7E-F).

claim: GRAMD1s are not essential for cell viability.
source: Using the CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing system, we demonstrated that GRAMD1s are not essential for cell viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful generation and maintenance of GRAMD1 TKO cell lines.

claim: Cells that lack all three GRAMD1s grow more slowly than wild-type cells.
source: Although cells that lack all three GRAMD1s grow more slowly than wild-type cells, they do not exhibit major abnormalities.
evidence: This is an observation from the characterization of TKO cells.

claim: PM lipidomics did not reveal major differences in PM cholesterol levels between GRAMD1 TKO cells and wild-type cells.
source: Accordingly, PM lipidomics did not reveal major differences in PM cholesterol levels between GRAMD1 TKO cells and wild-type cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-D).

claim: GRAMD1 TKO cells exhibited an exaggerated accumulation of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol in response to acute hydrolysis of sphingomyelin.
source: First, GRAMD1 TKO cells exhibited an exaggerated accumulation of the accessible pool of PM cholesterol in response to acute hydrolysis of sphingomyelin, which liberates the sphingomyelin-sequestered pool of cholesterol into the 'accessible pool'.
evidence: This is demonstrated by D4 binding assays and GRAM1b recruitment assays (Figure 4D-E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: GRAMD1 TKO cells showed reduced suppression of SREBP-2 cleavage upon hydrolysis of sphingomyelin.
